label: Blue Note
rationale: Jackie McLean's One Step Beyond is one session — April 30, 1963 at Rudy Van Gelder's studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey — released on Blue Note as BLP 4137, produced by Alfred Lion [S1,S2,S3,S4,S5] (obs). Consensus (signal 1): AllMusic rates it 5/5 (Thom Jurek: 'the first volley McLean fired in the direction of the new jazz ... still sounds fresh, vital, and full of grainy mystery') [S1,S2] (obs), and The Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide also gives it 5/5 [S1] (obs) — two independent listing traditions at the top mark. Lineage (signal 2-3): this is the record that opens the inside-out sequence McLean, Moncur and Hutcherson then carried forward, and both immediate successors are already in the canon — Destination... Out! (recorded 20 September 1963, same pianist-less format) and Grachan Moncur III's Evolution (1963) — so the influence is audible inside the collection, not asserted from outside [S3] (obs). Session gravity (signal 4): the date introduced four players to the wider record — Moncur, Hutcherson, bassist Eddie Khan and seventeen-year-old Tony Williams, who joined Miles Davis' quintet a month later [S2,S5,S7] (obs); Hutcherson describes the chain himself — McLean heard him at the Club Coronet, called Alfred Lion, 'so we all went off to Rudy Van Gelder's [studio]' [S7] (obs). Defining statement: McLean replaced the piano with Hutcherson's vibraphone for the first time here, the move that gave the band its open, spacious sound and made him a leader of the post-bop transition rather than a hard-bop stylist [S1,S5] (obs). It still plays (signal 5): four originals in 37:33, two by McLean and two by Moncur, with no filler; the LP is still the recommended entry to McLean's inside-out period [S1,S2,S5] (obs). The hole it fills: the canon holds Jackie's Bag (1960), Let Freedom Ring (1962) and Destination... Out! (1964) but not the 1963 record that began that arc — the sequence reads as if it started with its second instalment [S3] (obs, cross-checked against the DB). Dating note, recorded rather than smoothed: the session is unanimously 30 April 1963 [S1,S2,S3,S4] (obs); Blue Note issued the LP in January 1964 [S1,S5] (obs), and the dossier carries 1963 because the canon dates by recording year.

personnel_record.notes: One session: April 30, 1963, Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey — Englewood Cliffs, not Hackensack, because Van Gelder moved in July 1959 [S1,S2,S3,S4] (obs). A single quintet plays throughout: no substitutions, no guests, no piano [S1,S2,S3,S5] (obs). Production: Alfred Lion produced [S1,S2,S4,S5] (obs); Rudy Van Gelder engineered [S4] (obs), corroborated by the house pattern for Blue Note dates at his own studio — AllMusic's credits table lists him only as remasterer and prints no engineer credit [S2]. Track durations are Wikipedia's [S1] and sum to 37:33, matching the LP; the alternate take of 'Saturday and Sunday' (8:32) is a CD-reissue bonus and is flagged as such [S1,S4]. AllMusic gives the album's total playing time as 47:00, which is the CD program including the alternate [S2]. Label dating: recorded 1963, released January 1964 [S1,S5]. Streaming: the four-track Apple edition (collectionId 1444092985) is the original LP program; a five-track Rudy Van Gelder Edition (716042948) carries the alternate [S6].

ballot.case_for: The April 30, 1963 session is a consequential hinge: McLean’s piano-less quintet with Bobby Hutcherson and Grachan Moncur III opens the inside-out sequence that continues in *Destination... Out!* and Moncur’s *Evolution*, both already in the canon (S3); Hutcherson’s account of McLean bringing him to Blue Note adds first-person context for the session’s formation (S7). The date also captures seventeen-year-old Tony Williams shortly before he joined Miles Davis, while AllMusic and the *Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide* each give the album 5/5 (S1, S2).
ballot.case_against: The album’s strongest musical and historical case overlaps substantially with *Destination... Out!*, which the references describe as the more mature realization of the same pianoless quintet language; the canon may already represent that sound through the later album. The consensus evidence is also narrow: the dossier cites two high ratings but no Penguin Guide, JazzTimes, or other broad cross-tradition recognition, so it does not establish overwhelming consensus.
ballot.disagreement: One reference judges the lineage and session-gravity case strong but keeps the album contested because of redundancy and limited consensus sourcing; the other considers it consensus core, arguing that its historical role makes it an indispensable companion rather than a duplicate.
ballot.recommendation: John should consider it a strong, contested addition that fills a meaningful gap in the McLean sequence, while weighing whether *Destination... Out!* already carries enough of that musical story.
